analysis.one_liner: Lets the FTC enforce antitrust laws against tax-exempt hospital systems.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee since April 2025 with no committee vote, no floor action, and no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal antitrust enforcers currently have limited reach over nonprofit hospitals, even though many of the largest and fastest-consolidating hospital systems are nonprofits. This bill would change the Federal Trade Commission's legal definition so that tax-exempt hospital organizations and cooperative hospital service organizations fall under FTC competition enforcement. That would give the FTC a new tool to challenge hospital mergers and other conduct that reduces competition, which research links to higher prices for patients and insurers.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients, employer health plans, and taxpayers who pay hospital prices. Hospital consolidation has repeatedly been associated with higher prices in local markets, so giving the FTC authority to challenge anticompetitive deals by nonprofit systems would help anyone who bears those costs, including people with private insurance and communities facing reduced service after mergers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and employers paying hospital prices

how_it_helps.text: Amends the FTC Act's definition of 'Corporation' so that tax-exempt hospital organizations and cooperative hospital service organizations (501(c)(3) groups) are covered by FTC antitrust authority.
The bill is titled the 'Combatting Hospital Monopolies Act', indicating its purpose is to address monopoly power in hospital markets.

analysis.who_pays: Tax-exempt hospital systems and hospital cooperatives, which would lose their exemption from FTC competition enforcement and could see planned mergers or acquisitions challenged, blocked, or unwound.

drawbacks.text: Hospitals argue that mergers can preserve rural and struggling community hospitals that cannot survive independently, so broader FTC authority could complicate rescues of financially fragile facilities.

The bill is a one-line jurisdictional fix with no safeguards, funding, or rural-hospital carve-outs, so opponents could fairly argue that a more careful bill would separate anticompetitive consolidation from genuine hospital rescues.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is real and large for anyone who pays hospital prices, since nonprofit systems make up much of the hospital industry and consolidation has repeatedly driven prices up. The cost falls on hospital systems that would face more scrutiny of their mergers. The bill's weakness is design, not goal: it is a bare jurisdictional change with no protections for legitimately struggling rural hospitals, which is likely the strongest good-faith objection.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in late April 2025 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a vote, or any cosponsor since.

narrative.text: Rep. Victoria Spartz introduced the bill on April 24, 2025.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and no further action has been taken.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tax-exempt hospital systems are better off so far, because the measure that would subject them to FTC merger enforcement has not moved, and hospital consolidation continues unimpeded by new federal scrutiny.

for.name: Rep. Victoria Spartz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its only public support so far; no House member has cosponsored it.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill in the months since referral.

sides.party_line_note: With a lone Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, there is no record yet of how the parties would line up.

industries.note: The bill would strip their practical exemption from FTC antitrust enforcement, exposing consolidation strategies to federal challenge. Hospital consolidation is associated with higher prices for patients and insurers, so the industry's interest here runs against the people who pay hospital bills.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employers who pay hospital prices
industries.note: More competition enforcement against dominant hospital systems could lower the hospital prices insurers and self-insured employers negotiate. Those savings are largely passed through to premium payers.

analysis.trajectory: With no cosponsors, no hearing, and no committee action since April 2025, this bill is very likely to die quietly in committee when the 119th Congress ends, like most single-sponsor first-intro antitrust bills.
